name: Oreate AI
tagline: Browser dashboard that bundles generative video, image, and voice tools behind one credit balance.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Tools in this shape are almost always a polished queue, gallery, and billing layer sitting on top of models somebody else trained and hosts. An agent can rebuild that layer for one person in a sitting: a prompt box, a job queue, a results grid, local storage of every output. What it cannot rebuild is the inference, so your personal version becomes a thin console over fal, Replicate, or an OpenAI-class API, with your card attached instead of theirs. That is fine if you generate occasionally and want your files on your own disk, and worse if you generate constantly, since bundled credit pricing can beat raw per-call rates. Call it a kinda: the UI is trivial, the thing doing the work is rented either way.
coreLoopDIY: A local web console where you pick a model, submit a prompt, watch the job finish, and keep every generated file plus its parameters in a searchable library on your own disk.
requirements: Node 20 and a local Postgres or SQLite
API key for a hosted inference provider such as fal.ai or Replicate
A payment method on that provider, since inference is not free
Disk space, since video outputs get large fast
whatYouLose: Bundled credits, which may be cheaper per generation than paying an inference API directly
Any model the service hosts privately or has fine-tuned and does not expose through a public API
Prompt presets, aspect ratio and style pickers, and the curated model list that saves you reading docs
Hosted storage, sharing links, and anything that works from your phone without a tunnel
Someone else absorbing provider outages, model deprecations, and silent API changes
moatNotes: The defensible part is prepaid GPU capacity and a model menu that stays current, not the interface.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because generative media is a buffet problem: people want to try six models without opening six accounts, reading six pricing pages, and discovering that one of them bills per second of output. Paying one subscription to get a working queue, sane defaults, and a single credit meter is worth real money to anyone whose job is output rather than plumbing. The DIY console is genuinely nice if you have settled on one or two models and want your files local and your prompt history intact. If you are still exploring, you will spend your weekend on provider onboarding instead of generating anything.
notes: The console is a one-sitting build; the GPU bill shows up either way.
prompt:
Build a local-first generative media console called Studio. One user, no accounts, runs on my machine.

Stack, no substitutions: Next.js 15 App Router with TypeScript, Tailwind, SQLite via Drizzle ORM, and the fal.ai JS client for inference. Store files on the local filesystem under ./storage, never in the database.

Features that are in scope:
1. A model registry defined in a single TypeScript file: each entry has an id, a human label, a media kind of image, video, or audio, the fal endpoint, and a zod schema for its inputs. Seed it with one text-to-image model, one text-to-video model, and one text-to-speech model.
2. A generate page: pick a model, render a form from that model's zod schema, submit. Show estimated cost if the registry entry declares one, otherwise say unknown.
3. A jobs table in SQLite with status of queued, running, done, or failed. Submit to fal, poll for completion in a server route, download the result bytes to ./storage, and write the local path back to the row. Store the full input payload as JSON on every job so any generation is reproducible.
4. A library page: grid of outputs, newest first, filter by media kind and model, free-text search over prompts. Click an item for a detail view with inline preview, the exact input JSON, a copy-params-to-new-job button, and a delete that removes both row and file.
5. A spend page: total calls and total declared cost per model per month, read straight from the jobs table.

Out of scope, do not build: user auth, teams, sharing links, cloud storage, payment handling, telemetry, model training or fine-tuning, and any model hosting of your own.

Rules: FAL_KEY lives in .env.local and is read only on the server, never shipped to the client. Fail loudly with the provider's error message when a job fails, do not retry silently. Write a seed script and a README that explains how to add a model to the registry in under ten lines. Include the SQLite file and ./storage in .gitignore.
